title: Why “I Understand You” Can Sometimes Be More Suffocating Than Not Being Understood
deck: The most closed kind of understanding is not getting someone wrong, but believing the person before you can no longer revise what you know about them.
body: Being misunderstood hurts.
We want those close to us to see the reasons behind our actions, to know why a sentence went unspoken, and to know that a decision was not as simple as it appeared.
So “I understand you” is usually reassuring.
But sometimes it can also feel suffocating.
Not because understanding itself is a problem, but because another meaning hides behind the words: I already know what kind of person you are, so you no longer need to explain.
You say you are simply tired, and the other person replies, “You always do this when you’re afraid to face a problem.”
You say you want to change the plan, and they say, “I know you. You’re just being impulsive for the moment.”
You express a new wish, but the other person uses who you were to explain who you are now.
Whatever you say is put back into a story that is already complete.
Understanding then ceases to be a way of drawing close and becomes a way of closing things off.

The better someone knows us, the more easily they accumulate a set of explanations about us. They have seen how we react under pressure, know which experiences have left their mark, and know where we often hesitate. This knowledge certainly has value.
A relationship cannot begin each day as though we were strangers.
The question is whether past knowledge still allows the person here now to bring something new.
If every new account can serve only as evidence for an old explanation, the other person has not really heard you. They are merely using your words to keep proving a conclusion they reached long ago.
Even objections can be absorbed.

The more you say, “It isn’t like that,” the more they think you are being defensive; the harder you try to explain that you have changed, the more convinced they become that you have not yet recognized your true self.
An understanding that cannot be refuted cannot be tested either.
It seems profound because it can explain everything. Precisely because it can explain everything, it no longer needs to face the person before it.

What feels most suffocating is not that someone has misread us, but that they have claimed a position from which only their interpretation can explain us, while even our own account becomes mere material.
This is sometimes called “knowing you better than you know yourself.”

At certain moments, this may be true. People can fail to see their own habits and use convenient reasons to conceal real motives. Those close to us may indeed point out things we are unwilling to acknowledge.
But pointing out a blind spot is not the same as permanently owning the right to interpret.
A helpful observation says, “I’ve seen you pull back at similar moments several times before. Could that also be a factor this time?”
A closed interpretation says, “This is just how you are, so what you’re saying now cannot be trusted.”
The first brings an observation before the other person and waits for a response. The second has already supplied their response for them.
Understanding someone requires a measure of certainty, but also room for uncertainty.
A relationship with no accumulated knowledge cannot develop trust. Saying “I don’t know who you are” every time would also make someone feel they had never been remembered.
But truly knowing someone is not a fixed portrait.

It is more like an understanding continually revised: I remember how you chose before and know you may repeat those choices. At the same time, I acknowledge that the person you are today can give new reasons that change my judgment of you.
Loving someone cannot mean loving only the person we already know how to explain.

People change, sometimes slowly and sometimes suddenly. They may relinquish a goal that once mattered or begin to value something they used to overlook. If a relationship allows them to change only within familiar bounds, what is called understanding becomes a contract about who they must be.
“You can’t do that. It isn’t like you.”
Sometimes these words come from concern. They may also be asking another person to keep sustaining the order within our understanding of them.
But someone need not always resemble the person we knew in order to prove that the past was real.
Of course, change cannot automatically cancel responsibility.

Someone cannot say “I’m no longer who I was” and make all their past commitments and the consequences they caused disappear. Others also have the right to judge by long-term behavior rather than immediately believe a single new account someone gives of themselves.
Leaving room for change does not mean abandoning evidence.
It simply means refusing to turn evidence into a life sentence.
The feeling of being truly understood is often not “The other person can finally predict my every step.”
It is this: they listen with everything they already know, yet still allow who I am this time to change what they know.
The best meaning of “I understand you” is not “There is no part of you left that I do not know.”
It is:
“I am willing to draw close to you through the past, and willing to get to know you anew when you no longer fit that past.”
This kind of understanding does not eliminate unfamiliarity.
It simply stops unfamiliarity from automatically becoming a threat.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
